Read-only Git branch hygiene

Know what can be cleaned up before you delete it.

A repository with hundreds of stale branches has two kinds of ref in it, and they look identical in a branch list: the ones whose work is already on the default branch, and the ones holding the only copy of something. This page sorts a snapshot into both, in your browser. It never deletes anything and it never says a branch is safe to delete — it says which ones a human still has to look at.

1. Paste a snapshot

Nothing scanned yet. Load the worked example to see how it reads, or paste your own snapshot.

2. Read the queue

Waiting for a snapshot

Every row is a review item. Even review-delete-candidate is a routing label for a human queue, not permission to delete a ref.

    BranchClassReview actionWhyCommits
    Nothing reviewed yet.

    Show the text report 
    
    
    
  
    

  
    
    
    Where a snapshot comes from
    
    
    The snapshot is produced on your machine, by you, from a checkout you already have. It needs commit ancestry, which a browser cannot read — so the scanner builds the file and this page reviews it. That split is deliberate: the person reviewing the queue does not need the checkout, a Git client, or an account.
    
    
    python3 src/branch_hygiene.py --repo /path/to/checkout --emit-snapshot > snapshot.json
    
    
    To resolve branches against real pull-request history instead of leaving them uncertain, export your own pull requests first with your own credentials and pass them in:
    
    
    gh pr list --state all --limit 500 --json headRefName,state,baseRefName > prs.json
python3 src/branch_hygiene.py --repo /path/to/checkout --pr-json prs.json --emit-snapshot > snapshot.json
    
    
    Then paste snapshot.json above. The scanner makes no network call of its own and has no account or API key; gh uses the credentials already on your machine. See is it safe to delete this Git branch?, or how this compares with the GitHub Branches page.
    
  
    

  
    
    
    What the six classifications mean
    
    
    Review, never guess. Every finding carries a non-executable review action. Ambiguity is reported as ambiguity rather than resolved into a delete list, and the CLI exits non-zero for it instead of pretending that zero means safe.
    
    
    Recoverable by design. The manifest preserves branch tips and commit ids so a reviewer can keep unique work before operating Git elsewhere.
    
    
    Runs where the data lives. Use a local checkout or your own CI. Repository names, branch names, commit messages, and file contents never enter an analytics service.
    
  
    

  
    
    
    Common questions
    
    
    Does review-delete-candidate mean the branch is cleared for deletion?
    
    
    No. It means the branch's pull request was merged and its tip is inside the recorded base history, which is the strongest evidence this tool can produce from a snapshot — and it is still a routing label for a human review queue, not permission to delete a ref. Nothing on this page deletes anything, and nothing on it can.
    
    
    Does exit status 0 mean every listed branch is cleared for deletion?
    
    
    No. A zero exit status only means the snapshot contained no unresolved shared, moved-tip, or uncertain finding under --fail-on-risk. Every finding still carries a review_action, which is a routing label for a human review queue, not permission to delete a ref.
    
    
    What does exit status 2 mean?
    
    
    A human must review at least one finding classified shared, moved-tip, or uncertain before any cleanup proceeds. It never means a branch is confirmed clear for deletion — it flags exactly the cases the scanner cannot resolve on its own. On this page those are the rows counted in the headline.
    
    
    Why does a branch with no open pull request show as "uncertain" instead of safe?
    
    
    Without pull-request metadata there is nothing to distinguish an abandoned branch from one whose work was never proposed anywhere, so a branch that is not merged and not explicitly marked protected is reported as uncertain rather than assumed abandoned. Pass --pr-json (exported once with your team's own gh CLI credentials) to resolve branches against their actual pull-request history instead of guessing from ref state alone.
    
    
    Why is a branch whose pull request merged still not a delete candidate?
    
    
    Because a merged pull request only tells you that some commits landed, not that the branch still points at them. If the local tip was moved after the merge — a rebase, an amend, one more commit — the tip is outside the base history and those commits exist nowhere else. That case is classified moved-tip, and it is the one this tool exists to catch: it is indistinguishable from a clean merge in a branch list. The worked example includes one.
    
    
    Does this tool delete branches or run any Git write operation?
    
    
    No. It only reads refs, commit ancestry, and the JSON files you pass it. It never fetches, pushes, or deletes, and the recovery manifest it writes explicitly marks itself read-only and approval-required. This page cannot reach your repository at all.
    
    
    Does repository data leave the machine it runs on?
    
    
    No. The snapshot you paste is parsed and classified entirely in this browser; nothing is uploaded and there is no server to upload it to. The scanner likewise makes no network requests. The optional --usage-log and this page's counting record only an aggregate event name and count — never branch names, commit messages, repository names, or file contents.

It is not legal, security, or compliance advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for meeting any obligation it helps you prepare for. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use, including deletion of a branch it classified.
    
    
    Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, export your inputs and run it yourself.
    
    
    Everything runs in your browser. Your data is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (scan_completed, example_loaded, report_copied, manifest_downloaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button above. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured. Support on GitHub Sponsors if this saved a unique branch — entirely optional, the tool stays free either way.

is-it-safe-to-delete-this-branch.html.text:
← Repository branch hygiene

Is it safe to delete this Git branch?

Every repository accumulates them: hundreds of refs, most of them merged long ago, a handful carrying work nobody remembers. Producing the list is a one-liner. Acting on it is where the damage happens, because the property that makes a branch safe to delete is not the one the list is usually sorted by.

Open the free branch hygiene scanner

Age is not the signal. Reachability is.

A branch untouched for a year whose commits are all reachable from the default branch is free to delete — the work is in main, and the ref is a label on history that exists anyway. A branch untouched for a year that carries commits reachable from nowhere else is the opposite: deleting the ref is the only thing keeping those commits addressable, and once the reflog expires they are gone in a way no amount of searching recovers.

Both branches look identical in a list sorted by last commit date. Sorting by "stale" is therefore sorting by the wrong column.

ClassificationWhat it means
Merged into the default branchNothing unique is lost. The cheap case.
Carries unmerged commitsDeleting drops the only reference to real work. Read it before deciding.
Ambiguous or malformed refFail closed. An unresolved ref is not a safe deletion.

Write the recovery manifest first

For every branch you intend to delete, record the name, the tip commit SHA, the last commit date, and the classification that justified it — before the deletion, not as a note afterwards. Recovering a branch is trivial while someone still holds its tip SHA and effectively impossible once nobody wrote it down. The manifest costs one command and is the whole difference between an undo and an incident.

Keep deletion a human decision

The scanner is read-only on purpose. It turns a portable snapshot into a report, a recovery manifest, and — for spreadsheet or ticket-based review — an approval-queue CSV of branch metadata and a review action per row. The export deliberately contains no shell commands: it cannot approve a deletion and it cannot perform one. For a scheduled or CI review it emits a stable JSON summary and can fail closed when the snapshot contains an ambiguous ref, so an unclear case stops the run rather than passing quietly.

Common questions

Is it safe to delete a stale Git branch?

It is cheap to delete a branch whose commits are already reachable from the default branch, because nothing is lost — the work is in main. It is not safe to delete a branch that carries commits reachable from nowhere else, however old or inactive it looks, because deleting the ref makes those commits unreferenced and eventually collectable. Age and inactivity say nothing about whether unique work exists; only reachability does, so classify on that and record the tip SHA of anything you delete.

What should I record before a branch cleanup?

A recovery manifest: for every branch you intend to delete, its name, its tip commit SHA, its last commit date, and the classification that justified the deletion. Recovering a deleted branch is trivial while you still hold the SHA and effectively impossible once nobody wrote it down and the reflog has expired. The manifest costs nothing to produce and is the difference between an undo and an incident.

Does this tool delete branches for me?

No, deliberately. It reads a snapshot you supply and emits a report, a recovery manifest, and optionally an approval-queue CSV containing branch metadata and a review instruction. It never contains a shell command, cannot approve a deletion, and cannot perform one. Deletion stays a decision a person makes with the report in front of them.

No warranty. This free page is not engineering, security, or operational advice, and it does not determine that any branch is safe to delete. Classification depends entirely on the snapshot you supply, which may be incomplete or out of date. Verify against the repository itself, keep the recovery manifest, and confirm with a qualified professional before deleting anything you cannot afford to lose. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free and experimental and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. Do not use this as a system of record.

vs-github-branches.html.text:
← Repository Branch Hygiene

This tool vs. the GitHub Branches page

Two different questions. GitHub's Branches page tells you how old a branch is and how far it has diverged from the default branch. This page tells you whether deleting it would destroy the only copy of something — which is the question you actually need answered before a cleanup.

What each tool is for

The GitHub Branches page is built into every repository on GitHub and included at no extra cost. It lists every branch with its last update and author, shows how many commits each branch is ahead of and behind the default branch, surfaces the pull request attached to a branch where one exists, and separates branches it considers active from ones it considers stale. It is also where branches are deleted, and where a branch deleted from that page can be restored. For seeing and managing what exists, it is the right tool and nothing here replaces it.

This scanner does none of that. It does not list your remote branches, show authorship, open a pull request, or delete anything — it has no token, no account, and no API access to your repository at all. It takes commit ancestry from a checkout (or from a snapshot exported from one) plus optional pull-request metadata you export yourself, and classifies each branch by whether its commits still exist somewhere else: merged, protected, active, shared, moved-tip, or uncertain. What comes out is a human review queue, a recovery manifest, and a CSV — never a delete command. It runs free in any browser or from a local checkout, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you paste.

The gap this exists to cover

A branch list sorts by age and by divergence, and neither is the same as “this work exists elsewhere”. Two cases in particular look entirely ordinary in any branch list:

A merged pull request whose branch tip moved afterwards. Merging tells you some commits landed on the base branch. It does not tell you the branch still points at them. One more commit, an amend, or a rebase after the merge leaves the tip outside the base history, and those newer commits may exist nowhere else — while the branch still reads as merged. This tool classifies that case moved-tip and keeps it out of the delete pile.

A squash or rebase merge. Both rewrite the branch's commits into new ones, so the originals are not ancestors of the default branch even though the work is fully landed. The ahead/behind count then reads as “ahead” on a branch that is genuinely finished. Classifying from ancestry plus recorded pull-request state, rather than from an ahead count alone, is what separates those from branches that really are the only copy.

And a branch that is old is not thereby abandoned, while a branch touched yesterday can be a duplicate of work that landed last month. Age is a useful filter and a poor verdict.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What branches exist, who last pushed to each, and which have open pull requests?The GitHub Branches page — built in, live, and authoritative about your remote.
I want to delete a branch, or restore one I just deleted.The GitHub Branches page. This tool cannot delete anything and never will.
Would deleting this branch destroy the only copy of some commits?This scanner — free, private, no account, classified from commit ancestry.
Its pull request merged, but has the tip moved since?This scanner's moved-tip classification, the case a branch list cannot show.
I have several hundred stale refs and need a reviewable queue, not a list.This scanner's report, recovery manifest, and approval-queue CSV.
I need the same review on GitLab, Bitbucket, or a self-hosted remote.This scanner — it reads a Git checkout, so the host does not matter.
I need this to run offline, or without granting any tool access to the repository.This scanner — it makes no network call and holds no credential.
What does “safe to delete” even mean for a Git branch?This tool's own worked explainer.
Do I need an account or a sign-in to use the tool?This scanner: no. The Branches page needs a GitHub account with access to the repository.

Most teams get different value from each: the Branches page for seeing and managing what exists and for actually performing a deletion, and a private read-only scanner like this one for deciding which of those deletions is safe to make. This page's own classifications are a review queue, not permission to delete a ref, and not a backup.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the classification runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this scanner or the GitHub Branches page?

They answer different questions, and most teams cleaning up a branch list will use both. GitHub's Branches page is built into every repository and is the fastest way to see what refs exist, who last pushed to each one, how many commits each is ahead of and behind the default branch, whether a pull request is attached, and which branches GitHub considers stale — and it is where the delete button lives, along with the restore option that undoes a deletion made from that page. This scanner does one narrower thing: it reads commit ancestry from a checkout, or from a snapshot exported from one, and sorts every branch by whether its commits still exist somewhere else. A branch whose pull request merged but whose tip moved afterwards, and a branch whose work landed under a different filename, look ordinary in any branch list; they are the two cases this tool exists to separate out. It runs free, keeps no account, uploads nothing, and never deletes or writes anything. A team that wants to see and manage branches is in the right place on GitHub; a team about to delete a few hundred of them and wanting to know which ones hold the only copy of something is in the right place here.

Does GitHub not already tell me a branch is merged?

It tells you a pull request merged, which is not the same claim. A merged pull request means some commits landed on the base branch; it does not mean the branch still points at those commits. If the tip moved after the merge — one more commit, an amend, a rebase — those newer commits are outside the base history and may exist nowhere else, while the branch still reads as merged. The same gap appears in the other direction: after a squash merge or a rebase merge the branch's original commits are not ancestors of the default branch at all, so an ahead/behind count can show a branch as ahead when its work is fully landed. This scanner classifies from commit ancestry rather than from merge state alone, and reports the moved-tip case separately instead of folding it into merged.

Does this tool delete branches or need access to my repository?

No to both. It only reads refs, commit ancestry, and JSON files you pass it — it never fetches, pushes, or deletes, and it has no token, no account, and no API access of its own. Its output is a review queue and a recovery manifest that marks itself read-only and approval-required. This comparison page cannot reach your repository at all, and the browser version classifies a snapshot you paste entirely on your own device.
